test_text.title: Silbo Gomero - the whistle 'language' of the Canary Islands

article.title: Silbo Gomero - the whistle 'language' of the Canary Islands

items.sentence_raw: La Gomera is one of the Canary Islands situated in the Atlantic Ocean off the northwest coast of Africa.
This small volcanic island is mountainous, with steep rocky slopes and deep, wooded ravines, rising to 1,487 metres at its highest peak.
It is also home to the best known of the world's whistle 'languages', a means of transmitting information over long distances which is perfectly adapted to the extreme terrain of the island.
This 'language', known as 'Silbo' or 'Silbo Gomero' - from the Spanish word for 'whistle' - is now shedding light on the language-processing abilities of the human brain, according to scientists.
Researchers say that Silbo activates parts of the brain normally associated with spoken language, suggesting that the brain is remarkably flexible in its ability to interpret sounds as language.

"Science has developed the idea of brain areas that are dedicated to language, and we are starting to understand the scope of signals that can be recognised as language," says David Corina, co-author of a recent study and associate professor of psychology at the University of Washington in Seattle.
Silbo is a substitute for Spanish, with individual words recoded into whistles which have high- and low-frequency tones.
items.explain: Q20: The passage says *'individual words recoded into whistles'* — **'individual words'** are the sounds in Spanish that get turned into tones. The question asks what the tones represent, and the answer is **words**.

items.sentence_raw: A whistler - or "silbador" - puts a finger in his or her mouth to increase the whistle's pitch, while the other hand can be cupped to adjust the direction of the sound.
items.explain:
Q21: The passage says a silbador *'puts a finger in his or her mouth to increase the whistle's pitch'* — the **finger** directly controls the pitch. The question asks what controls the pitch, so the answer is **finger**.

Q22: The passage says the other hand *'can be cupped to adjust the direction of the sound'* — so a cupped hand changes the **direction**. The question asks what is changed with a cupped hand, so the answer is **direction**.

items.sentence_raw: "There is much more ambiguity in the whistled signal than in the spoken signal," explains lead researcher Manuel Carreiras, psychology professor at the University of La Laguna on the Canary island of Tenerife.
Because whistled 'words' can be hard to distinguish, silbadores rely on repetition, as well as awareness of context, to make themselves understood.
The silbadores of Gomera are traditionally shepherds and other isolated mountain folk, and their novel means of staying in touch allows them to communicate over distances of up to 10 kilometres.
Carreiras explains that silbadores are able to pass a surprising amount of information via their whistles.
"In daily life they use whistles to communicate short commands, but any Spanish sentence could be whistled."
items.explain:
Q15: The passage says *'any Spanish sentence could be whistled'* — this means Silbo can handle **long and complex** messages, not just short ones. The question says Silbo is *'only appropriate for short and simple messages'*, which directly contradicts the passage. So the answer is **FALSE**.

Q23: The passage says *'In daily life they use whistles to communicate short commands'* — **'short commands'** are brief orders or instructions. The question asks for the transmission of brief what, so the answer is **commands**.

items.sentence_raw: Silbo has proved particularly useful when fires have occurred on the island and rapid communication across large areas has been vital.
items.explain: Q24: The passage says Silbo is useful *'when fires have occurred'* for rapid communication — **'fires'** are the emergency events. The question asks what information is relayed about, so the answer is **fires**.

items.sentence_raw: The study team used neuroimaging equipment to contrast the brain activity of silbadores while listening to whistled and spoken Spanish.
Results showed the left temporal lobe of the brain, which is usually associated with spoken language, was engaged during the processing of Silbo.
items.explain: Q16: The passage shows a clear difference: for silbadores, the *'left temporal lobe'* was engaged, but for non-whistlers, *'activation was observed in all areas of the brain'*. The question says they *'produced different results'*, which matches exactly. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: The researchers found that other key regions in the brain's frontal lobe also responded to the whistles, including those activated in response to sign language among deaf people.
When the experiments were repeated with non-whistlers, however, activation was observed in all areas of the brain.
items.explain: Q16: The passage shows a clear difference: for silbadores, the *'left temporal lobe'* was engaged, but for non-whistlers, *'activation was observed in all areas of the brain'*. The question says they *'produced different results'*, which matches exactly. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: "Our results provide more evidence about the flexibility of human capacity for language in a variety of forms," Corina says.
"These data suggest that left-hemisphere language regions are uniquely adapted for communicative purposes, independent of the modality of signal.
The non-Silbo speakers were not recognising Silbo as a language.
They had nothing to grab onto, so multiple areas of their brains were activated."

Carreiras says the origins of Silbo Gomero remain obscure, but that indigenous Canary Islanders, who were of North African origin, already had a whistled language when Spain conquered the volcanic islands in the 15th century.
items.explain: Q17: The passage says indigenous islanders *'already had a whistled language when Spain conquered'* the islands — this means Silbo existed **before** the Spanish arrived. The question says *'The Spanish introduced Silbo'*, which is the opposite. So the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: Whistled languages survive today in Papua New Guinea, Mexico, Vietnam, Guyana, China, Nepal, Senegal, and a few mountainous pockets in southern Europe.
There are thought to be as many as 70 whistled languages still in use, though only 12 have been described and studied scientifically.
items.explain: Q18: The passage says *'only 12 have been described and studied scientifically'* out of about 70 languages — this means data is **incomplete**, not precise for all. The question asks if there is *'precise data available regarding all'* whistle languages, which is not true. So the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: This form of communication is an adaptation found among cultures where people are often isolated from each other, according to Julien Meyer, a researcher at the Institute of Human Sciences in Lyon, France.
"They are mostly used in mountains or dense forests," he says.
"Whistled languages are quite clearly defined and represent an original adaptation of the spoken language for the needs of isolated human groups."
But with modern communication technology now widely available, researchers say whistled languages like Silbo are threatened with extinction.
items.explain: Q25: The passage says *'modern communication technology'* threatens Silbo with extinction — **'modern communication technology'** is the new tool that replaces whistling. The question asks what new thing threatens the future, so the answer is **technology**.

items.sentence_raw: With dwindling numbers of Gomera islanders still fluent in the language, Canaries' authorities are taking steps to try to ensure its survival.
Since 1999, Silbo Gomero has been taught in all of the island's elementary schools.
items.explain: Q19: The passage says *'Since 1999, Silbo Gomero has been taught in all of the island's elementary schools'* — **'elementary schools'** means schools for children. The question says *'children of Gomera now learn Silbo'*, which matches perfectly. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: In addition, locals are seeking assistance from the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO).
"The local authorities are trying to get an award from the organisation to declare [Silbo Gomero] as something that should be preserved for humanity," Carreiras adds.
items.explain: Q26: The passage says local authorities are trying to get *'an award from the organisation'* (UNESCO) — an **award** is a prize or recognition. The question asks what UNESCO thing they hope to receive, so the answer is **award**.

orphan_explain_map.14: Q14: The passage describes La Gomera as *'mountainous, with steep rocky slopes'* and gives its highest peak — but it never compares it to other Canary Islands. The question asks if it is the **'most mountainous'**, which requires a comparison. Since the passage provides no comparison, the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
